correctness.rationale: Independent exponentials are transformed to independent uniform edge priorities. Exact boundary vacancy recursion h_m=1−∫h_(m−1) gives the finite individual-edge integral and mean expansion with O(n^-1) at log n+x. Greedy acceptance has a strictly decreasing-priority ancestral path; the chance of crossing a radius-L window is at most 2/(L+2)!. Taking L=ceil(log n), Chen–Stein dependency neighborhoods of at most 4L+1 and two-late-clock joint probability bounded by e^-2t give O(log n/n) total variation. Mixed factorial moments of spatial and time-window rare counts give the full marked Poisson limit, and tail truncation yields the last-k interpretation. The actual included independent standard-library checker exactly verified 40 boundary probabilities, all 36 marginal edge probabilities across 46,233 chronological edge permutations on paths n=2..9, and 42,990 causal-window discrepancy witnesses. The proof, not the finite enumeration, establishes the infinite result.

originality.rationale: Primary-source comparison found a decisive 2002 precedent for the scalar Gumbel jamming law and treats that result as prior art. Gerin 2015 establishes the same RSA construction, time density, and first-order logarithmic trials but not a spatially marked Poisson extreme process or count error rate. Penrose–Sudbury 2005 normal-approximates occupation totals, and Purvis et al. 2015 treats near-jamming coverage scaling. Searches of published mathematical records and related literature found no dominating joint marked limit. Residual risk: the result could have been obtained or implicitly asserted elsewhere via known localization and Chen–Stein tools.

value.rationale: A published scalar Gumbel jamming-time law leaves the late deposition locations, multiplicities and joint arrival times undetermined. The product-form marked point-process limit answers this natural late-stage geometry question: the last fixed number of dimers have independent uniform limiting locations, with jointly ordered extreme times; the O(log n/n) count approximation provides finite-n calibration. The exact edge probabilities support the full structural result. This is motivated by the classical random deposition problem and is not just a new name for the known marginal Gumbel law.
